en: The Sutra on the Poor Old Man Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Shi Huijian.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was seated in a vihāra in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, together with two...
He was accompanied by a thousand bhikṣus.

At that time, there was an old man who was poor and destitute, two hundred years of age; his eyebrows grew with fine hairs, his ears protruded from his head, his teeth were as white as even shells, and his hands reached below his knees; when one looked at his appearance, he seemed to possess the marks of a noble person.

Yet, impoverished and suffering, his clothes could not cover his body; his five limbs were bare and his belly was constantly empty from hunger. As he moved with every step, he drew only a faint breath as he came leaning on a staff, desiring to see the Buddha.
Śakra and Brahmā were attending at the gate and had ordered that no one be admitted.
An old man then called out loudly, saying:

"Though I am poor and lowly, a mere commoner among the people, I have been fortunate for a thousand years to now encounter the Buddha. I wish to inquire about sin and merit, seeking liberation from all sufferings."

"I have heard that the World-Honored One’s benevolence reaches everywhere and that all things depend upon him; there is none who does not receive his grace. For this reason, I have come from afar to beg for a single audience.
Yet you have obstructed me; since you have both contravened my wish and erred regarding the Sage's intent, how could such a thing be appropriate?"
The Buddha, knowing this, looked toward Ānanda and said:
“Do you see that long-lived, elderly man with the marks of an old man whose transgressions are not yet exhausted?”
Ānanda joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How can one who possesses the auspicious marks of longevity and merit yet suffer the consequences of sin?
Does a person who has committed such sins still possess these marks?"
"Where is it now? It is something I have never seen since birth.
The Buddha said:
"He is nearby, outside the gate.
Śakra and Brahmā have cleared the way; you may call him forward.
Thereupon, the old man crawled forward inch by inch, prostrated himself before the Buddha, and with a mixture of grief and joy, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I am unfortunate to have been born into this world; impoverished, exhausted by toil, and afflicted by hunger and cold, I seek death but cannot find it, while living I have nothing to rely upon. Human life is most precious, and I cannot abandon it myself."

Hearing that the Buddha was still in the world, my heart was filled with singular joy; day and night I resolved my mind, vowing to behold his countenance. Ten years have passed since then, and only now have I achieved this fruit.
Previously, I stood outside the gate for a long time without being able to advance.

Calculating that I wished to return, my strength failed me; with no way to proceed or retreat, I feared only that my life would end here, defiling the holy gate and further increasing my transgressions.

If the Celestial Honored One has already taken pity on me in my lack of awakening, allowing me to advance further and not depriving me of my original vow, then to die in such a state would leave no cause for regret!
"I only wish to quickly bring my offenses to an end; in future lives, I pray that you will bestow your grace upon me and grant me your supreme wisdom.
The Buddha said:
"When a person undergoes birth, the causes and conditions of birth and death arise from manifold factors, thereby resulting in the roots of transgression."
Now I shall explain its origin for you.
In a previous life, you were born into the family of a wise and noble king of a powerful and great nation.
At that time, as a crown prince, your pride and nobility were extraordinary; you were beloved by your parents above and revered by your ministers and subjects below.

Using this license to treat others with contempt, he casts haughty glances and looks down upon them with arrogance; though his wealth and treasures amount to hundreds of millions, they all belong to the people.
"The common people are impoverished, all because of the tax levies; they know only how to amass wealth and refuse to practice giving.
At this time, there was a poor and humble śramaṇa named Jingzhi who came from a distant land and has come specifically to visit you. His request is not great: he seeks only a Dharma robe."

Yet you were utterly improper and treated me with extreme hostility; you neither offered me clothes nor gave me food, but sat there empty-handed before me, refusing even to let me depart when I wished to leave.
For seven days and nights, he has been completely deprived of water and food; yet he still draws breath, his life hanging by a thread.
When you see this, you instead rejoice greatly, gathering people to watch him, taking it to be a source of pleasure.
A courtier standing nearby admonished the minister, saying: "Do not act thus toward the Crown Prince! This śramaṇa is compassionate and respectful;

his virtue and Way are harmonized within him. Even if he were frozen, he would not feel cold; even if he were starved, he would not feel hunger. The reason he comes to beg is simply that he wishes to cultivate merit."
"Since I have not bestowed anything upon him, how can I be pressured to do so?
I pray you release him, lest you incur his sin. The Prince replied:
"Who is this person who falsely claims to possess the Way and its Virtue? Let us test him by causing him a slight hardship, but only enough to keep him from dying.
If we release him after that, there will be no cause for concern."
He was immediately sent away and driven out of the country.
Before he had even crossed the border, after traveling some ten or more li, he encountered hungry bandits who wished to kill and devour him.
The śramaṇa said:

"I am a poor and freezing śramaṇa, emaciated and reduced to a mere skeleton; since my flesh is both putrid and foul-smelling, it is unfit for consumption. I shall merely be killed in vain, serving no purpose."
The famished bandit spoke again:
"I have been exhausted by hunger for many days and have been eating nothing but earth; though you are somewhat thin, you are nonetheless flesh.
I will certainly not let you go; you must simply face death."
Thus they vacillated back and forth for a long while in confusion.
When the Prince learned of this, he went to rescue them, saying:
"Since I am unable to beg food and clothing for them, would it truly be right to let the bandits kill them?"
When the bandits saw the prince, they all prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground, confessed their transgressions, and apologized for their crimes, then released the śramaṇa to go.
"The śramaṇa at that time was none other than the present-day Maitreya Bodhisattva;
the noble and esteemed prince was you yourself."
Therefore, Minister, you now undergo this retribution of poverty because you sat upon stinginess and greed;
yet the reason you have attained long life is that you saved the lives of the śramaṇas.
"The retribution for sins and blessings is also like a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound.

The old man said to the Buddha, "My past deeds are already as they are; I wish to conclude my affairs now. I beg to receive this remaining life of mine to become a śramaṇa, and in all future births, may I always attend by the side of the Buddha."
The Buddha said, “Excellent!

At that moment, the old man’s hair and beard fell to the ground; dharma robes appeared upon his body, his physical vigor was restored, and his ears and eyes became sharp and clear. He immediately attained supreme wisdom and entered the gate of samādhi.
He praised the Buddha with these verses:
"In the past, when I was a crown prince, I did not understand the principles of benevolence and righteousness.
Arrogant and self-indulgent due to my noble status, I relied upon being the great king."
Thinking oneself free from both sin and merit, one might believe this state can be maintained forever;
yet how could one have realized that amidst the opposition of birth and death, one would now suffer its calamities?
From sin, one may again receive blessings, and thus come to behold the God among Gods.
Able to shed past transgressions, They enter the Dharma-gate at the end of their lives;
Forever free from the mind of stinginess and greed, They long enjoy the root of wisdom.
Life after life they attend the Buddha’s side, Preserving it through ten thousand kalpas.
Thereupon, the elderly bhikṣu, having spoken this verse, paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
This concludes the *Sūtra of the Poor Old Man* as spoken by the Buddha.
